articles.title: CMA Awards Predictions: Expect Ella Langley to Get Everything but Male Vocalist, and Maybe Even That's Not Safe
articles.summary: The suspense is unbearable: Will the 2026 CMA Awards see Ella Langley enjoying a total sweep, or just a near-sweep? That is a real question, not a rhetorical one. But before we start trying to anticipate the math, let's remember that, although Langley had a leading nine nominations, the most she can win is seven, […]
articles.content:
The suspense is unbearable: Will the 2026 CMA Awards see Ella Langley enjoying a total sweep, or just a near-sweep?

That is a real question, not a rhetorical one. But before we start trying to anticipate the math, let's remember that, although Langley had a leading nine nominations, the most she can win is seven, because she is competing against herself in two categories, single of the year and song of the year, where “Choosin' Texas” is up against “Be Her.” Normally that would leave room for vote-splitting, but rest assured, Langley and her two-stepping two-timers have the means to overcome that little problem. So with best single and best song utterly in the bag, that leaves five more open to see if she can run the board with the Country Music Association's voters.

Entertainer of the Year, especially? There is some real suspense there. In some matters, it does take a crystal ball to see.

Here are our predictions for the winners of the 60th annual awards, which air live from Nashville's Bridgestone Arena from 8-11 on the east coast and delayed for prime on the west coast, also at 8.

Luke Combs Cody Johnson Ella Langley Chris Stapleton Lainey Wilson

Will win: Ella Langley Could win: Cody Johnson

This top honor used to be regarded as something closer to an ongoing lifetime achievement award for a currently hot superstar than a recognition of pure, recent artistic achievement that could go to someone in the earlier stages of a long ascent. But it felt like that was starting to change when Lainey Wilson got it in 2023 without having developed any severe road wrinkles. (She also got it again in 2025.) All of which is to say that there is a question that could be asked with Lainey and this honor: “Too soon?” And the likely answer to that is: “Nope, but thanks for asking.”

Still, there is a lane open here for anyone to bust through if voters should decide that an armful of “lesser” awards are good enough for Langley this year. No one would greatly begrudge the well-love Wilson getting it for the third time in four years. Combs is probably the longest shot, being a two-time winner, like Langley. Neither Stapleton nor Johnson have gotten it even once. Stapleton has the “seriously, overdue” factor in his favor, having been nominated 11 times without ever taking it home. But if the enthusiasm for keeping it fresh continues but it's just not Langley's time for it, Johnson feels most like a presumptive second-place — and possibly first-place — finisher.

Still, the vast mainstream/crossover audiences watching the show at home will scratch their chins if it's anyone but Langley, who has two of the biggest songs of the year in any genre in “Choosin' Texas” and “Be Her” and has undoubtedly become country's biggest ambassador to the world for this particular time frame. Choosin' anyone else would just seem strangely insular.

"Be Her" – Ella Langley "Choosin' Texas" – Ella Langley "I Knew It, I Knew You" – Taylor Swift "Somewhere Over Laredo" – Lainey Wilson "The Fall" – Cody Johnson

Will win: "Choosin' Texas” Could win: Get real. Are you insane?

If “Choosin' Texas” didn't exist, we might be supposed that Langley would still be a front-runner for the award, but for “Be Her.” According to data provided to Variety by Luminate, “Be Her” is the all-around third most-consumed song of 2026 among all genres, not just country. But “Choosin' Texas” is one of the biggest hits (use your Kanye voice here) of all time , as it currently enjoys a record-extending 28th week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Moreover, there is no resentment in the country community against its success, and certainly none against Langley for crossing over when the song America can't stop falling for is as country as country can be. Seeing a shoo-in get shooed in never felt any better.

Ain't In It For My Health – Zach Top Dandelion – Ella Langley Middle of Nowhere – Kacey Musgraves Parker McCollum – Parker McCollum The Way I Am – Luke Combs

Will win: "Dandelion" Could win: "Parker McCollum"

It's hard to imagine the scenario where an album as across-the-board as good as “Dandelion” doesn't follow “Choosin' Texas” into the winners' circle. But there's a case voters can reasonably make for casting their ballots for anything else in the category. Musgraves' “Middle of Nowhere” was the most critically acclaimed country album of the year overall, and marked a definitive return to country after some musically farther-afield records from the star. It would be wonderful to see Kacey finally get it, many of us can agree. But only occasionally do voters go for an album that didn't have a huge impact at mainstream country radio, as evidence by the fact that Musgraves' often left-of-center approach has landed her four prior nominations in this category but only one win (for “Golden Hour”).

Still, this is the category where voters are most apt to sometimes break ranks with bestselling stuff and pick something cool to make a statement. (Think Lee Ann Womack's “There's More Where That Came From” in 2005.) So that could mean it's back to being Musgraves' time… or it could mean they'd have a hankering for Parker McCollum's critically acclaimed, self-titled album, in which he was seen as going for artistry more than hits. The fact that the ACM Awards gave McCollum this award back in the spring definitely should be taken into account in reading the tea leaves. But realistically, it just seems like we'll never know which of those albums came in second… because how can Langley lose?

SONG OF THE YEAR Award goes to Songwriter(s)

"Be Her" Songwriters: Smith Ahnquist, Michael Hardy, Ella Langley, Jordan Schmidt "Beautiful Things" Songwriters: Jessi Alexander, Jessie Jo Dillon, Connie Harrington, Megan Moroney "Choosin' Texas" Songwriters: Luke Dick, Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Joybeth Taylor "Dry Spell" Songwriters: Luke Laird, Shane McAnally, Kacey Musgraves, Josh Osborne "Gary" Songwriter: Stephen Wilson Jr.

Will win: "Choosin 'Texas" Could win: Get real, again.

It's hard to remember when the CMA Awards had a greater crop of songs up for this honor than this year. Can they make it a five-way tie and everyone gets a prize? No, they cannot. So as much applause as we might want to hold in reserve for Musgraves, Megan Moroney or Stephen Wilson Jr., this particular prize has had Langley's name on it since before the creation of the world. Not to get biblical.

Miranda Lambert Ella Langley Megan Moroney Kacey Musgraves Lainey Wilson

Will win: Ella Langley Could win: No other option. The need to get real persists.

If you were making a list of the five most outstanding artists in country music in the 2020s, you could pick these five without any shame or need to move on… even if we might eventually worry we'd overlooked a guy or two. But honestly, what a field. Anyway it's Langley's to lose.

Luke Combs Cody Johnson Chris Stapleton Zach Top Stephen Wilson Jr.

Will win: Ella Langley. No, just kidding. Cody Johnson Could win: Stephen Wilson Jr.

We should probably look at which three artists from this field are also nominated for entertainer of the year, and narrow it down from there. Of those three, Johnson has the freshest momentum, even though Combs and Stapleton are not a bit less popular than they ever were. You could never go wrong with virtually anyone in the world by naming Stapleton the male vocalist of this or any year, but he might have simply won it too many times. It would be a news-making upset if Wilson should get in — the odds are really stacked against him amid these proven heavyweights, but there is so much appreciation for him that a big cheer would go up if he crashed through that ceiling.

Lady A Little Big Town Midland Old Dominion The Red Clay Strays

Will win: The Red Clay Strays Could win: Old Dominion

The vocal group and vocal duo categories tend to have the least fresh blood and the most predictable year-by-year streaks The Red Clay Strays were a surprise winner last year — no one was more surprised than them — so it'll be interesting to see if that was a one-off or the start of yet another CMA streak. I'm betting the latter, not least of all because they're basically a rock group, and country people love having a real rock group — a good one — to bring some rootsy energy and fierceness into the genre.

Brooks & Dunn Brothers Osborne Dan + Shay Muscadine Bloodline Thelma & James

Will win: Brooks & Dunn Could win: Brothers Osborne

Just as much as CMA voters have liked having some new blood to vote for, in the form of the Red Clay Strays, they have enjoyed going back to Brooks & Dunn to celebrate old-home week. They've won this 16 times, and finally returned to the winners' circle last year after previously last getting it in 2018. Their comeback as awardees here still feels fresh, in that sense, even if it's a feat as old as time immemorial for them.

"A Song To Sing" – Miranda Lambert (with Chris Stapleton) "Horses and Divorces" – Kacey Musgraves (feat. Miranda Lambert) "I Can't Love You Anymore" – Ella Langley & Morgan Wallen "If I Don't Leave I'm Gonna Stay" – Carly Pearce & Riley Green "McArthur" – HARDY, Eric Church, Morgan Wallen & Tim McGraw

Will win: "I Can't Love You Anymore" Could win: "Horses and Divorces"

This one is actually a tough category to call. The Langley/Wallen duet will probably get swept in on the wave that is pushing Ella toward so many other noms, and there continues to be support for Wallen in many pockets of the industry, even though you wouldn't know it from the lack of nominations he's gotten since winning entertainer of the year two years ago. But although their song served its purpose as something for them to sing together on his tour, is it really up there with Langley's best songs or more of an agreeable time-passer? If it should fail to ride through on her long coattails, it's tough to know where things go from there. I'm partial to the sensual Pearce/Green duet, and wish Pearce was up for a lot more for her excellent album.

But damn it, “Horses and Divorces” actually was an event, if you're going to take the title of the trophy seriously. After a long, low-simmering feud no one denied, Musgraves had the brilliant idea to call Lambert up for a peace-pipe session, in the guise of a songwriting section about their feud … to great comedic-yet-real effect Talk about working it out on the remix. As Clint Eastwood once said, though, deserve's got nothin' to do with it. So expect Langley to need to build an extra shelf.

"Choosin' Texas" – Ella Langley "Dry Spell" – Kacey Musgraves "Gary" – Stephen Wilson Jr. "The Fall" – Cody Johnson "White Horse" – Chris Stapleton

Will win: "Choosin' Texas" Could win: "Dry Spell" or "Gary"

“Choosin' Texas” isn't really the most interesting video of all of these, but it gets the job done, and that should be enough to have it two-step its way into the winners' circle. Still, maybe this is the place for voters to exercise a fondness for Musgraves, via her amusing video about sexual frustration in the supermarket. As Freud said, sometimes a cucumber is not just a cucumber.

Avery Anna Carter Faith Emily Ann Roberts Tucker Wetmore Stephen Wilson Jr.

Will win: Tucker Wetmore Could win: Stephen Wilson Jr.

Wetmore is the only one here with No. 1 hits, which ought to be enough to push him across the line as voters face the inevitable question of how they think their choice will hold up 10 or 15 years from now. He'd be a worthy winner, but so would any of the others, most of all the critically beloved Faith and Wilson. Faith just picked up a key Grammy nomination… which of course means little in this context, but just saying… she's interesting and she's a keeper. So is Wilson, who has a much larger profile at present, including a lot of left-over love from how he killed it on last year's telecast, twice. Wetmore is the horse to bet on, but this might be closer to a photo finish than most would suspect.

articles.title: Leading Cyber Expert: “We Are Entering the Flickers”
articles.summary: Former Defense Department Cyber Czar Brett J. Goldstein says Hollywood and media are about to get pummeled along with everyone else.
articles.content: One hallmark of living in late-stage 2026 is the possibility that we'll wake up and the news site we visit is down, or trying to steal our money. If we muster the courage to get out of bed, we shouldn't expect to talk to anyone or go anywhere, as chances are that Outlook is offline or the FAA has grounded flights . Perhaps a bleak portrait, but one that has been painted in the past week with a host of cyber-security fails — “an advent calendar of societal collapse,” as Jon Stewart put it on The Daily Show Monday night. A slew of those fails have affected the media and entertainment worlds already, with CNN part of said crypto-swipe Tuesday morning and plenty of executives and workers stuck on the ground Friday. So far cyber experts don't believe anything coordinated is happening here, even if some cable-news figures aren't so sure . But even without a single unifying bad actor, the picture is bleak. Fading infrastructure combined with new AI tools that can easily exploit it can only spell trouble. For an industry still scarred by the 2014 Sony hack and all it exposed, the news hits hard. And Hollywood conducts a lot more business digitally these days than it did then, from all the Fandango ticket-ordering to the Spotify-streaming to the Disney+-subscribing. Cyber attacks and a faulty Internet hold the possibility of a major industry disruption. So how worried should the business — and we as individuals — actually be? For that we called Brett J. Goldstein. Goldstein (no relation to the Richmond barker, oi) holds an esteemed perch in American cyber defense, having occupied the role of director of the Defense Digital Service in the DoD under late-era Trump I and early Biden. He's also a former Chief Information Officer for the city of Chicago and currently holds a professorship at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, where he runs a lab examining such threats. We caught up with him by Signal Tuesday. For anyone looking at all the failures and groundings in the past week, it can be hard not to connect the dots. Do you see them as related in any way or the result of one actor? I don't know that there's reason to believe its coordinated but it's certainly a scary sequence of events which is very troubling. The loss of email or problems with Chase or groundings at United — just because it's not coordinated doesn't mean it's not a cumulative problem. What are the roots of that problem in your view? What we are seeing is an under-investment in our infrastructure that is coming home to roost. You used to be able to hide — it used to take a determined researcher to find a security weakness. But now thanks to AI we can't really hide. AI can find a needle in a haystack as never before. And so we have weaknesses as never before. Just look at PHP (a failure in Internet code baked-in during the 1990s that has been unearthed by AI). So we have to start fixing all of it, and we can't put it off even one day. It feels like we have spent decades eating poorly and now, facing a potential heart attack, we're trying to avoid it with a crash diet. Is this possible to fix quickly? I don't know that it's impossible but it's certainly true we have a lot of sins to pay for. We need to pay our tech debt. There really are only two scenarios: the next few years will be either bumpy or really freaking bad. Everyone needs to change the way they're thinking to make sure it's the first one. So a best-case scenario is bumpiness. What does that look like? I think we are entering a period of the flickers and I think this past week has really demonstrated that. My sense is this is the beginning. You wrote in a Washington Pos t op-ed last week about those flickers. “For you, it looks like this. Your bank's app is down. The pharmacy cannot pull up your prescription. Your paycheck is late — not stolen, just late because the payroll company unplugged its system to be safe. None of it is a catastrophe on its own. All of it, every week, is a different country from the one we live in now." That is what will happen and all we can do is start fixing things across various sectors to shorten the period it happens. And [AI] frontier labs need to be a part of the solution too. If we bring quality [solutions] and stability we can make it less bumpy. But I don't think we can avoid that we are entering the flickers. So we just need to start updating our systems. What does that mean for individuals? This feels like good advice if you run an IT department but what about as consumers? Signal over text, obviously. But what about everything else? Is clicking on CNN actually bad? Is my credit card exposed just because it's on file at Hulu? Should we all just be moving to clay tablets? I would just say do all the things you're supposed to do and don't put it off. If a Chrome update button pops up for the love of Job click the freaking button. If there's a patch, install it. Two-factor authentication and strong passwords and passkeys of course. If there's something more complicated in your life consult a cyber expert. You need to do all of the steps, not some of the steps, not most of the steps. Noting is foolproof but there are ways to protect yourself more. Many people in the entertainment industry are especially worried because they still feel the aftereffects of the Sony hack. I talked to someone recently who was exposed and the way they spoke can only be described as a kind of PTSD. How likely is something on that scale happening again? I think there's a lot of variance in the media sector just like there is in all sectors. Some companies and some individuals are reasonably protected and vigilant. And then with others it's like “Oh my God, you're so high profile and you're not taking care of business." But if the question is it more likely or less likely, of course it's more likely. A few years ago when you thought about [a hack] it needed to be an adversary with a lot of tenacity and effort. Now AI-enabled scenarios make it so someone with no scruples can, without much effort, look at 100 things at once. The business side of Hollywood seems at risk as well. Streaming services rely on smooth digital interactions to conduct business; even a few seconds is critical, never mind compromised data or a daylong outage. How vulnerable are all those platforms? This is super-impactful for commerce. My core point if you're in a position to do something at an organization is to set priorities. Yes you can do all the fancy front-facing AI stuff you're doing but if you're not doing the other stuff — if you're not making sure the underlying platform is fundamentally sound and sustainable — none of that matters. OK, I've been putting it off. You've gotten into the bumpy scenario. What's the really freaking bad one? Well, I'll just say your whole day is tied to a system, and what happens if that system starts to unravel? If you can't trust it? If it's not just about a grounded flight which forces you to drive but everything else? But again, it's an inflection point for us as a society. It's not too late. We do have a choice.

articles.title: Here's How to Play GTA 6 Early Ahead of Its Official Release Date and Unlock Time
articles.summary: After years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally releasing this week on Thursday, November 19th. Despite having been announced by Rockstar Games all the way back in 2022, anticipation for the latest Grand Theft Auto sequel started simmering long before. As such, for fans to be on the cusp of being able to […]
articles.content:
Despite being nearly at the finish line, there are undoubtedly millions of Grand Theft Auto fans who are finding these final days before release to be the most grueling. Fortunately, for those who can't bear to wait roughly 36 hours for Grand Theft Auto 6 to begin unlocking in their own region, there is one major loophole that will allow users to play the game earlier on November 18th. If you want to take advantage of this trick for yourself, the process of doing so is relatively simple.

Since Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released at 12:00am local time in each country and region around the globe, this means that the game will see a staggering launch. Simply due to how time zones work, players in New Zealand will be able to jump into GTA 6 for themselves first, with the game then proceeding to unlock in Australia, Japan, and other countries around the globe in the hours to follow. As luck would have it, though, anyone around the globe can briefly become a resident of New Zealand, which will allow them to play the game in advance of its unlock time in their own country.

To accomplish this feat for yourself, all you have to do is navigate into your console's settings menu and find the “Language and Location” option. From here, change your location to New Zealand and then reset your console. Once this is done, your console will then identify as being in New Zealand, which will grant you access to GTA 6 the moment it launches in the region. Specifically, this would be at 6am ET/3am PT for those in the United States.

The only disappointing caveat with this New Zealand method, however, is that it only works on Xbox Series X and S consoles. This means that those planning to play Grand Theft Auto 6 for themselves on PlayStation 5 won't be able to use this exploit. Given how many more players the PS5 version of GTA 6 will undoubtedly have, the majority of fans will instead have to simply wait until 12am on November 19th to begin experiencing the game.

It's also worth noting that there's no guarantee that this New Zealand workaround on Xbox Series X/S will end up working with Grand Theft Auto 6 . Although this trick typically works on just about any and every game released on Xbox platforms, Rockstar Games has been notoriously secretive with GTA 6 and has done quite a lot to ensure that it wouldn't leak or launch before it's supposed to. Whether or not this means that the New Zealand method has been fixed for the arrival of GTA 6 isn't yet known, but it's something we'll find out about soon enough.

articles.summary: Before "Avengers: Doomsday," there was "Avengers: The Kang Dynasty." Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige announced the latter title at Comic-Con in July 2022, with Jonathan Majors' Kang the Conqueror poised to become the Marvel Cinematic Universe's next Thanos-sized villain starting with 2023's "Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania." Those plans, however, were upended a few weeks […]
articles.content:
Before “ Avengers: Doomsday ,” there was “Avengers: The Kang Dynasty.” Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige announced the latter title at Comic-Con in July 2022, with Jonathan Majors' Kang the Conquerer poised to become the Marvel Cinematic Universe's next Thanos-sized villain starting with 2023's “Ant-Man and the Wasp Quantumania.”

Those plans, however, were upended a few weeks after “Quantumania” opened in theaters and earned some of Marvel's worst reviews and box office. Majors was arrested in March 2023 after he assaulted his then-girlfriend in the backseat of a private vehicle. The actor was officially convicted in December 2023, with a six-person jury finding him guilty of two misdemeanor counts of harassment and assault. Marvel did not hesitate to cut ties with him, firing Majors immediately after his conviction was announced. The actor was then sentenced in April 2024 to one year of domestic violence counseling. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Jon Stewart Weighs In on Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Casting: ‘You Already Got Batman’ 'You Can See Everything' Sparks Frenzy in Europe as Screenings Sell Out and Anticipation Soars: 'People Are Just Desperate to See It'

With Majors' firing, the Marvel Cinematic Universe would be overhauled with “Avengers: The Kang Dynasty” being replaced by “Avengers: Doomsday.” The plan now moved to bringing back Robert Downey Jr. to the MCU, only this time not as Iron Man (who died in 2019's “Avengers: Doomsday) but as the villainous Doctor Doom. However, Marvel Studios boss revealed in the latest issue of Empire magazine (via The Playlist ) that Doom was in the conversation to be added to the MCU well before “The Kang Dynasty” fell apart amid Majors' legal troubles.

"It probably would still have been called ‘The Kang Dynasty,' but it would have been a set-up for Doom, midway through that movie," Feige said, revealing the plan for “The Kang Dynasty” was actually for it to be a bait-and-switch movie in which Doom was revealed as the real Thanos-sized villain of the MCU's multiverse sage. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

According to Feige, Marvel first got in touch with Robert Downey Jr's agent (telling him: “We have an idea, it's time”) around the same time as the “Quantumania” premiere in February 2023, weeks before Majors' arrest in New York City.

"It was very delicate," Feige added about the Majors situation. "We didn't want to rush into any rash decisions in terms of employment. People think there was a cause-and-effect with Jonathan's issues, and that certainly accelerated some things. But the Doom of it all was well underway before that… ‘Quantumania' was not received the way we would have liked. There are many elements of that that we're proud of, the Kang performance being one of them. But we were changing [‘The Kang Dynasty'] even at that point."

articles.title: The Next Bond Villain: From Idris Elba to Kristen Stewart, 22 Actors Who Should Face Off Against Robert Pattinson
articles.summary: Every James Bond is only as good as the person who’s trying to kill him. Throughout the franchise’s history, we’ve seen Sean Connery take on Gert Fröbe’s Goldfinger, Roger Moore tackle Christopher Walken’s Max Zorin and, in the Daniel Craig era, Mads Mikkelsen’s Le Chiffre in “Casino Royale” and Javier Bardem’s notorious Raoul Silva in […]
articles.content:
Riz Ahmed is skilled in dramatic roles, like his Oscar-nominated performance as a troubled drummer in “Sound of Metal.” But he’s also a master of voice and motion-capture acting, from Severus Snape in the “Harry Potter” audiobooks to the ruthless symbiote leader Riot in “Venom.” So whether he plays it straight or perhaps takes the form of a monstrous menace to Robert Pattinson’s Bond, Ahmed has the subtle, steely power to be a baddie either way.

Pierce Brosnan led four James Bond films as the titular superspy in the late ’90s, so why not bring him home for one last ride as the silver-haired supervillain?

Brosnan, who was vocal throughout the 007 casting process, has remained a staple of the action genre 24 years after his final turn as Bond in “Die Another Day.” He recently lent his espionage expertise to Steven Soderbergh, playing the double-agent villain in his twisty spy thriller “Black Bag.” Also on the villain front, Bronsan has been stirring up trouble as the leader of the Irish mob in “Mobland,” which is wrapping its second season.

Director Denis Villeneuve is about to bring Timothée Chalamet through his villain arc in “Dune: Part Three,” and he may want to bring that tyrannical overlord energy with him to the Bond franchise. Chalamet, like Robert Pattinson, is one of Hollywood’s most in-demand stars, which makes him an intriguing on-screen rival. Chalamet has built his young career playing righteous leading men, however complicated they may be, in films like “Marty Supreme,” “A Complete Unknown” and “Wonka.” It could be time for Chalamet to stay on the dark side for a bit longer and take on cinema’s suavest spy.

If Pattinson made his case for playing Bond with Nolan’s time-bending spy thriller “Tenet,” then Debicki should also be strongly considered alongside him. The two of them had standout roles in the movie, and we’re dying for them to get some more screen time together. “He is an enigma himself,” Debicki told Variety about Pattinson’s Bond casting. “He’s beautiful, and he’s funny and he’s smart. I think he’s perfect. I’m so thrilled.”

Having spent so many years being tipped by the media for the 007 job — and then being asked about Bond in every interview — it feels only right that Idris Elba be given a juicy bad guy role to play. But this is no consolation prize for the Brit, who has excelled in intimidating, scene-commanding villainy on more than one occasion, including as the brooding and calculating Stringer Bell in his “The Wire” breakout, the ruthless mercenary leading a group of child soldiers in “Beasts of No Nation,” the genuine action movie baddie in “Hobbs & Shaw” and, er, the master criminal feline Macavity in “Cats.” OK, fine.

Colin Farrell has already gone toe-to-toe with Pattinson, buried under prosthetics as Oz Cobb in “The Batman.” The Oscar nominee from “The Banshees of Inisherin” has played a hit man with a conscience in films like “In Bruges” and an assassin as Bullseye in “Daredevil.”

Now let's picture that Irish charm curdling into something far more dangerous, like an arms baron who’s a blast to watch even as he’s trying to kill Bond. Do it.

Fassbender spent years playing an empathetic villain in Fox’s “X-Men” series as a young Magneto. Now, he’s played a suave spy in last year’s surprise sleeper hit “Black Bag,” a cold assassin in David Fincher’s 2023 thriller “The Killer” and a CIA officer in “The Agency” on Paramount+. He certainly fits the bill to star in a Bond movie, perhaps as a double-crossing 00 spy who faces off against Pattinson.

Rebecca Ferguson has shown she can keep up with Tom Cruise’s Ethan Hunt in the “Mission: Impossible” franchise, so it could be time for her to face off against cinema’s other iconic man of mystery.

Outside of her three “Mission” films, she recently took on internal affairs as a high-level situation room officer in Kathryn Bigelow’s “House of Dynamite.” Ferguson is probably best known for her leading role in Apple TV’s “Silo” as Juliette Nichols, a mechanic-turned-post-apocalyptic liberator. It also helps she’s in Denis’ orbit already with the “Dune” franchise.

She’s already a pro at unraveling a conspiracy, so she is sure to be an expert at weaving one together in the face of Bond.

Walton Goggins is already one of Amazon's most valuable assets, starring in Prime Video's post-apocalyptic drama “Fallout” as a 200-year-old zombie cowboy.

Of course, Goggins made Boyd Crowder, the silver-tongued soul of FX's crime drama “Justified,” one of his most memorable creations. Plus, he nearly stole the show on HBO's anthology series “The White Lotus” as the haunted Rick.

Some of the best Bond villains are a little unhinged and completely charming, and Goggins brings both.

Villeneuve and Gyllenhaal have already worked together on “Prisoners” back in 2013, and they’re long overdue for a reunion. Gyllenhaal has played a wide variety of unsettling bad guys in recent years, like a grimy journalist in “Nightcrawler,” a theatrical Mysterio in “Spider-Man” and a smooth-talking criminal in “Ambulance.” He’s also bulked up and trained in UFC fighting for two “Road House” movies. His Bond villain could mix all of these past roles into one and be a true chameleon.

Isn't it safe to say that AMC's “The Night Manager” was pretty much Tom Hiddleston's 007 audition tape?

He reprised his role as former British intelligence operative Jonathan Pine earlier this year in the second season streaming on Prime Video. However, the tuxedo never came, so maybe being another scene-stealing bad boy can get him into the fold. As Loki in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Hiddleston proved audiences will adore a villain even while he betrays everyone.

Maybe casting him as a disgraced MI6 golden boy, or an agent who was supposed to get the number but then didn’t, will let him spend the whole movie proving he actually deserved it.

Angelina Jolie has already shared the screen with one 007 when Daniel Craig played her rival in “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider” (2001). What if she took a shot at the next one?

The Oscar winner of “Girl, Interrupted” has played both sides of the spy game in films like “Salt” and “Mr. & Mrs. Smith.” She also gave Disney one of its most iconic villains in the live-action format with “Maleficent.”

Let her bring a menacing rage to the MI6 team and watch what happens.

Daniel Kaluuya is reuniting with his “Judas and the Black Messiah” director, Shaka King, on a new Amazon MGM movie, “The Parlay,” so technically he's already in the family, right?

For anyone who saw Steve McQueen’s “Widows,” they’ll remember how terrifying the Oscar winner can be as he played the enforcer Jatemme and delivered one of the most chilling henchmen of the past decade. Let’s not forget “Black Panther,” where he played W’Kabi, the trusted friend who betrays his king.

Once thrown out as a worthy contender to play Bond, this Londoner, with his knack for exuding menace, would have MI6 very worried.

Barry Keoghan has already said that, rather than Bond, he’d prefer to play the villain. Still, he’s certainly got the credentials to prove it. From a sinister teen who embarks on a campaign of revenge in “The Killing of a Sacred Deer” to a swaggering, volatile gangster in “Calm with Horses” to the murderous manipulator of “Saltburn,” the Irishman has shown he could be 007’s perfect, cherubic master of menace. And then there’s that deleted scene in “The Batman” as the Joker opposite Pattinson. Time for a proper face-off between the two.

From Nolan to Villeneuve, Murphy could follow Robert Pattinson from one major director to another. Murphy hit the lotto with his “Oppenheimer” Oscar win, and playing a Bond villain could be his second wave. We know he’s up to the challenge after seeing him as J. Robert Oppenheimer, the Scarecrow in “Batman Begins” and Tommy Shelby in “Peaky Blinders.” Aside from a cameo in “28 Years Later: The Bone Temple,” Netflix’s “Peaky Blinders” movie and a return in “A Quiet Place 3,” Murphy’s slate has been too quiet since “Oppenheimer” and a Bond movie would be the perfect big-screen welcome back.

Upon learning that Pattinson would be Bond, Pitt pitched himself to play the villain at his “Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” premiere. Pitt has produced “Mickey 17” and “The Lost City of Z,” both of which starred Pattinson, so the two already have a connection. “I love what he’s been doing. I love his choices. I think he’s the real deal. That’s good. A good call, I like it,” Pitt said, then threw his hat in the ring to play the bad guy. “I’d like to do that. My man Javier [Bardem] did it so well. It’s tall shoes, but I’d take that on.”

Nobody in Hollywood makes politeness more terrifying than Jesse Plemons.

He was Todd, the soft-spoken killer of AMC’s crime series “Breaking Bad.” In Alex Garland’s “Civil War,” he turned one question, “What kind of American are you?“ into one of the frightening scenes of the year, in a one-scene wonder, no less.

A Bond villain who never raises his voice and never apologizes before he pulls the trigger. That's what exactly Plemons does best.

The Oscar nominee of “The Power of the Dog,” who won Best Actor at Cannes for “Kinds of Kindness,” is playing Plutarch Heavensbee in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” this year, a role originated by the late Philip Seymour Hoffman. And famously, also played a villain in “Mission: Impossible III” (2006).

Florence Pugh may be on many fans’ lists as a potential Bond girl (and so did Variety ), but it seems the Brit — who stars alongside Robert Pattinson in “Dune: Part Three” — would rather go a different route. Speaking at Elle’s Women in Hollywood event shortly after 007 was cast, she said she’d messaged Villeneuve to say: “Congratulations on finding your Bond, nice catch. Any villains the size of a 5ft 4in female?” While Pugh’s roles haven’t yet seen her dip into full-scale global terrorism, as Cathy in the recent “East of Eden” adaptation, she has shown she could certainly explore her darker side.

With his shape-shifting ability to transform into a menacing clown or a cadaverous vampire, Bill Skarsgård can become just about any villain the Bond creative team imagines.

Skarsgård’s roles in “It,” “Nosferatu,” “Barbarian,” and “The Crow” are just a few of the horror-tinged roles he's inhabited, suggesting his take on a Bond villain could lean more toward the grotesquely menacing side. The Swedish actor even appeared with Robert Pattinson, a fellow famous vampire, in the Netflix movie “The Devil All the Time,” though they didn’t share any scenes.

As soon as Pattinson’s name was floated as 007, hordes of Twihards were immediately fan-casting Stewart to give the Bond universe a “Twilight” crossover. But instead of playing a Bond Girl, Stewart would be a much more entertaining choice as a villain. Please, Amazon MGM, make this ultimate Bella Swan and Edward Cullen fan fiction come true. Better yet, cast Taylor Lautner as a henchman to Stewart’s Bond villain.

A great James Bond villain is known for their striking, singular presence – and who better to provide that presence than Tilda Swinton? Her otherworldly, androgynous persona has been put to good use by everyone from the Avengers to Wes Anderson, Bong Joon Ho and the Coen brothers, and she could easily switch on the evil vibes as a Bond villain. Swinton hasn’t worked with Robert Pattinson yet, but Pattinson is a big admirer of her performance in 2008’s “Julia.” “I think that’s one of the great performances, and it’s kind of criminally underseen,” he told Rotten Tomatoes.

In “I'm Still Here,” Fernanda Torres played Eunice Paiva, a woman standing up to a military dictatorship and the role earned her a Golden Globe statue and an Oscar nomination for best actress. While on the awards circuit, the Brazilian star knew exactly what she wanted to do with her next big venture: play a Bond villain.

“I would love to be the secretary of a James Bond villain,” she said on the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast . “And just say, ‘He will be waiting for you in the next room, Mr. Bond.’ That’s it. That’s my dream. Just this line. That’s all I want to do.”

Imagine Torres as the power behind the throne: a Rio de Janeiro media baroness who smiles for the cameras while quietly buying off half the government?

articles.title: Wait, The Actual Contestants On The Mob Weren't Told The Rules?
articles.summary: My mind is officially blown.
articles.content:
There are few things I love more than a reality show, and after years of devouring The Traitors with my Peacock subscription , I was thrilled to hear that the folks behind that Emmy-winning series were creating another. Enter The Mob , another campy competition show that's available in its entirety with a Hulu subscription . The show once again proved that RuPaul's Drag Race alum Willam Belli is a top-tier TV personality , but it turns out that not even the cast knew the rules when cameras went up.

Well, my mind is blown. It was hard enough to nail down the rules and format of The Mob as a viewer, but the fact that the cast was similarly clueless is truly wild to me. It didn't make the show's first four episodes any less entertaining, even though many of my favorite contestants got whacked way too early . Still, I'd think that the powers that be on production would want the reality TV personalities to at least know everything about the game they were expected to play.

Willam might be the only contestant from RuPaul's Drag Race to get disqualified, but that doesn't mean she went against the rules in every situation. After all, The Mob cast were starting a brand new competition series, and didn't have any previous episodes to use as a reference. The folks who caught on seemed to make it the farthest, but it was curtains for other favorites like Willam, Bruno, and Debi Mazar.
